awd_titl_txt: EAGER: NAIRR Pilot: Applying NAIRR Pilot Resources to Optimize AI-Ready Data Investments
awd_abstract_narration:
This EAGER project will demonstrate how National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (NAIRR) Pilot resources can facilitate the development of a new service to the cybersecurity research community, specifically to infer the utility of datasets and software tools based on their documented use in scientific publications. The service will enable the assessment of scientific data utility to address a growing need in the scientific research community: optimizing AI-ready data investments. The research will help funding agencies optimize investments in AI-ready datasets, provide a scalable model for other similar scientific disciplines, and enhance the broader research community's ability to evaluate and sustain valuable data resources. 


State-of-the-art techniques for automatically extracting links between resources cannot handle the complexity, variability, and contextual nuances of natural language, e.g., in discerning a reference to a resource from its use in a paper.  This project will require data collection, preprocessing and labeling, model selection and training, as well as evaluation and deployment.  The approach will leverage techniques such as prompt engineering and fine-tuning to extract relevant metadata from unstructured text, and associated inference of relevant annotations. The research will utilize multiple NAIRR compute resources and aims to provide a repeatable, AI-based method for inferring the utility of datasets and software tools. This capability will enable more accurate interpretation and explanation of complex relationships in scientific publications.  The resulting service will address a persistent and growing cybersecurity research challenge, and serve as a model for other disciplines.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Scientific progress increasingly depends on shared research resources: large data sets and software tools that many different research teams use in their work. These resources are expensive to collect, curate, and maintain, and data sets prepared for use with artificial intelligence (AI) will be even more costly to sustain. Funding agencies and research organizations therefore need reliable ways to determine which data sets and tools genuinely contribute to scientific discovery, so they can direct limited resources toward the investments with the greatest impact. Today, however, measuring the real-world use of a research resource is surprisingly difficult. The most direct evidence lies in the scientific literature itself, but published papers describe the resources they rely on in highly variable, informal language. In particular, existing automated techniques cannot reliably distinguish between a paper that merely mentions a data set and one that actually uses it to produce results. Making that distinction requires interpreting the context and meaning of natural language, a task that until recently was only feasible through slow and expensive manual review.

This project developed and evaluated a new approach to this problem using large language models (LLMs), which are well suited to handling the variability and nuance of natural language. The team, based at the Center for Applied Internet Data Analysis (CAIDA) at the University of California San Diego, designed a complete workflow that takes in scientific publications, identifies the data sets and software tools referenced in each paper, matches those references against a list of resources of interest, and determines whether each resource was actually used in the research or only mentioned in passing.

The project produced three concrete outcomes. First, the team created a high-quality benchmark data set: 46 research papers from the 2023 ACM Internet Measurement Conference, paired with a manually curated record of nearly 1,300 resource instances. For each resource, this record captures its name, the quotations citing it, the associated references, and whether it was actually used or merely mentioned. Second, the team implemented an end-to-end pipeline — from ingesting publications through model execution to results analysis — that identifies data sets and software tools in papers and classifies whether each was actually used. On papers the system had never seen during development, its determinations agreed closely with those of human expert annotators, correctly identifying roughly nine out of ten resource uses with few false alarms. Third, the project produced practical knowledge about how to apply LLMs to this task, gained through systematic experiments comparing different ways of prompting the models and evaluating four state-of-the-art openly available models. Extensive error analysis highlighted the subtle nuances of some cases and the overall complexity of inferring resource utility in scientific text.

 

The intellectual merit of this work was in demonstrating how modern AI language technology can perform context-aware extraction and interpretation of complex relationships from unstructured scientific text, a capability beyond prior automated techniques. The project produced a formalized workflow for resource extraction and matching, a curated benchmark data set for evaluating such systems, and practical findings about model selection and prompt design for this class of problems.

The broader impacts of the project extend across the research enterprise. The capability developed here will improve the quality of data and services that CAIDA provides to the cybersecurity and Internet research communities, helping researchers discover data sets, understand how others have used them, and get started with Internet data more quickly. The project also supports evidence-based decision-making by funding agencies, which must prioritize investments in data infrastructure. This work was conducted as part of the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (NAIRR) Pilot program.
